conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in today because of blurry vision and low blood pressure, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My vision in the left eye has been blurry since I woke up after that procedure last time. And I felt really weak after dialysis today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You had a venogram recently for your dialysis access, and you woke up with blurry vision then. Did it hurt or was there discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain or discharge. Just blurry, like I need reading glasses all of a sudden. And I’m already blind in my right eye from that shingles outbreak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The ophthalmology team saw you in the ER and said your vision is correctable with a +2.75 lens. They think it’s from the anesthesia affecting your eye’s ability to focus, not a serious problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it should get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should improve over the next few days. They recommend over-the-counter reading glasses for now and a follow-up eye exam within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it was something worse, especially with my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were concerned too, especially since you’re already monocular. But the exam was normal, so it’s likely temporary. Now, your blood pressure was very low in the ER—58 over 38. You got some fluids. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. No dizziness or lightheadedness now. But I haven’t been taking my midodrine since the last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. Midodrine helps with low BP during dialysis. We restarted it, and your pressure has been more stable—84 over 49 earlier. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it regularly. I just forgot after everything that happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. We’ll make sure it’s on your discharge list. Now, you mentioned trouble swallowing this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, felt like food was stuck in my chest. I’ve had that before—last time it was a yeast infection in my esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and HIV, that’s a real possibility. We’re starting you on fluconazole—200 mg today, then 100 mg daily for 14 days—to treat suspected candidal esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that medicine helped last time. Should I expect side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. Maybe some mild nausea. We’ll watch for that. Your HIV meds are continuing as before—Abacavir, Atazanavir, and the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My CD4 was low last time—27. Is that still a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it shows your immune system is still weak, which is why infections like MRSA and candida are more likely. We’re continuing your HAART to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin for the MRSA from my old catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still getting vancomycin with each dialysis. That’s a four-week course—last dose will be in a few days. We’ll confirm with your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my new catheter in the left groin—is it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did see some clotting in it during dialysis, which is concerning. You’ve had multiple failed accesses, and the venogram showed IVC stenosis, which makes clotting more likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what are we doing about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started warfarin—4 mg daily—to prevent clots. You’ll need to get your INR checked during dialysis and keep it between 2 and 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never been on blood thinners before. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your meds—no major interactions. And given your atrial fibrillation and ESRD, the benefits outweigh the risks. Cardiology supported this decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your lactate was high yesterday—3.2—suggesting poor perfusion from low BP. But it’s down to 1.8 this morning, so the fluids and midodrine are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My vision feels a little clearer today too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great to hear. Keep using the reading glasses. Any improvement in swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. No more sticking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign the fluconazole is working. We’ll keep you on it for the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound yesterday showed no fluid collection around your catheter. The swelling we saw is improving, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Blood cultures were negative. The swelling may be from irritation or mild inflammation, but it’s getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eosinophilia? Any new answers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still under investigation. It could be related to your advanced HIV or an allergic process. You’re scheduled to see dermatology and allergy as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had so many skin issues lately—itching, rashes. Maybe they can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on dialysis this morning—no issues with the catheter. Your INR came back at 2.4, which is perfect. Keep taking the warfarin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if everything stays stable. Your vision is improving, swallowing is better, BP is stable on midodrine, and your labs look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to see your PCP, get your INR checked during dialysis, finish the fluconazole, and follow up with ophthalmology, dermatology, and allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my GYN? I still have some discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last smear was negative for infection, but you should get a Pap smear as an outpatient. We’ll send a reminder to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable, and you’ve improved in all areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Just to confirm—I keep taking midodrine, warfarin, fluconazole, and vancomycin with dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you have fever, chest pain, vision worsens, or any bleeding. Otherwise, keep all your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
